description: We are Palafito Labs (Chiloé). We have built a mission simulator for young astronauts: a crew travels to the Space Station and tends to a crop of *Fragaria chiloensis*—Chile’s native strawberry—with support from mission control and a satellite, through games played on mobile devices, PCs, and in virtual reality. We use real NASA data and clearly label what is simulated. We are looking for expertise in graphic design, animation, video production, education, and science
summary: Space education usually shows children the results of a mission, not the decisions behind it. AMAYA (Adaptive Modular Architecture for Youth Apprenticeship) is an open, modular mission engine that turns a classroom into mission control. Students aged 7 to 12 become the crew of a simulated journey from Earth to Mars and must balance life support, radiation shielding, power, food production and communication delay. Every choice has a cost. Decisions are informed by real NASA open data, and every screen states what is REAL, SIMULATED or FICTION. AMAYA was built in Quemchi, a rural island community in Chiloé, Chile, and it runs offline on a laptop, a projector and the phones a school already has. Its first mission, Aucar, carries local culture on board; any other community can load its own Cultural Content Pack and Pedagogical Curriculum Pack without rewriting the engine. Under the hood, one laptop serves the whole room with no internet: every device is a vote that updates one shared mission file.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AMAYA is a classroom mission simulator. A teacher runs the mission from a command console while students play as flight crew, ground control, and data and knowledge teams. Each role has its own tasks. Before every critical step, the ground consoles hold a GO / NO GO poll, and the crew commander decides.

The trade-offs are the game. In the Mars segment, students face choices where no option is free:

- Communication delay: asking Earth for help takes time, so the crew must decide alone. The game shows the real Earth-Mars signal delay next to its compressed in-game delay.

- Radiation: a solar storm is coming. Students read real space weather data and choose where the crew shelters and sleeps.

- Food and resources: with limited actions per day, native potato yields more food but grows slower; white strawberry yields less food but raises crew morale. Oxygen, water, power and food all move with each decision.

HOW IT WORKS

AMAYA separates three layers that never mix:

1. Core engine: rounds, oxygen, water, food, power, radiation, seeded events, delayed messages, roles and team scoring. It is deterministic, so a class can replay the same mission and compare decisions.

2. Cultural Content Pack: the story, characters, crops, events and glossary of a place, written as plain text files.

3. Pedagogical Curriculum Pack: learning goals, activities, rubrics, pre and post assessment, and a teacher guide.

New games plug in as one more JavaScript file that registers itself in the engine; nothing else is rewritten.

Students join through whatever the school has: phones, computers, a projector, a Meta Quest headset, or a cardboard viewer. Virtual reality is a highlight, never a requirement. Everything is a web page: no installs, no accounts, no internet needed during play. Empty roles are covered by scripted bots.

TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE (built for a venue with no internet)

- One laptop runs Apache + PHP 8 (XAMPP) and serves the whole room over a local router: phones, computers, the projector and Meta Quest headsets. No internet, no server room, no installs.

- A single file, estado.json, is the source of truth for the mission. One PHP router (api.php) handles more than 70 actions, and flock() file locking stops simultaneous writes from many students from corrupting it. No SQL database is needed.

- No WebSockets, because shared hosting does not allow them: every screen polls the server every 1 to 2 seconds. A tap on a phone sends a short HTTP request, PHP checks the rules and rewrites the state, and the projector's three.js scene redraws.

- The projector pages (cine3d.php, viaje.php) only read the state and render NASA 3D Resources models. The teacher console (orquestador.php, lib/auto.php) can force or automate stages.

- A local cache (sat.php) downloads NASA GIBS imagery, space weather and orbital elements before the event, and serves the saved copy if the connection drops, labeled REAL, SIMULATED or FICTION.

- VR games are autonomous WebXR nodes over local HTTPS: heavy physics, such as 96 solar panels, runs on the headset with three.js, and achievements return to the student's phone through pasaporte.js and localStorage.

The design mirrors the pedagogy: many small inputs move one shared state, like a minga.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND HARDWARE

PHP 8, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, Python; three.js, WebXR, satellite.js (SGP4), esbuild; Apache via XAMPP; JSON files with flock(); Piper text-to-speech. Hardware: one laptop, a Wi-Fi router, a projector, the students' phones, Meta Quest headsets and cardboard viewers.

MISSION AUCAR

Our first mission was written in Quemchi. AUCAR station is named after Aucar Island, the Island of Sailing Souls. A crew from Chiloé travels to Mars carrying the native white strawberry in twin boxes: one stays on Earth as the control. Local knowledge becomes engineering: the palafito, a house on stilts, inspires a raised greenhouse above a buried habitat, and the minga, Chiloé's tradition of community work, is the game mechanic: nobody finishes the mission alone. Women lead the crew, to give girls role models in STEAM.

WHAT IS BUILT

- Mission V3: a 23-scene classroom mission for phones, projector and ground consoles, with radio, logbook, five guided experiments and scripted bots.

- Four browser-based VR experiences: Estación AUCAR, AUCAR ALMA (spacewalk) and Caleuche Órbita (robotic arm and sea temperature analysis), built on NASA 3D models, plus Odisea Solar (solar panel repair in orbit). They run on Meta Quest, on a phone inside a cardboard viewer, or on a plain screen.

- The AMAYA core engine with automated tests, a package validator, two cultural packs (Chiloé and a generic lunar base) and a base curriculum pack.

- A prototype Mars colony farm game.

WHAT IS NEXT

- A no-code mission manager so teachers can plan and edit missions (today packs are edited as text files).

- Connecting Mission V3 to AMAYA packs.

- An eight-stage learning program designed to run over eight months.

- Classroom trials. We have not yet measured learning outcomes, and we do not claim any.

WHY IT MATTERS

Quemchi is about 70 percent rural, with island schools that have a single teacher and patchy connectivity. AMAYA is designed for exactly that reality, and for any other: the story changes, while the engine and the science stay.

All AI characters in the story (Chucao, Minga IA, TARS) are scripted bots, labeled as such, and used to teach critical thinking about AI. This is an unofficial community project; the use of NASA data does not imply NASA endorsement.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): solar flares of the last 7 days. Used as the real context for the solar storm decision
NASA JPL orbital elements: positions of Earth and Mars, used to compute the real Earth-Mars signal delay shown next to the game's compressed radio delay.
Mars 2020 Perseverance raw images: a recent surface photo shown on arrival at Mars
NASA Trek: Mars map tiles, stored locally, where each player marks a hypothesis
NASA GIBS / Worldview: satellite imagery of Chiloé and Earth (MODIS, VIIRS)
NASA EPIC (DSCOVR): full-disk images of Earth
NASA 3D Resources: models of the International Space Station (interior and exterior), EMU suit, Canadarm2, spacecraft and rovers, used in the three VR experiences
NASA Image and Video Library: photographs used in the mission gallery
projectRefs: NOAA SWPC: Kp index, solar wind and aurora
